sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Zmey ​Gorynych** ‌(*zmeygorynych*) — ‌Three-Headed ​Dragon ​· ​Mountain ​dragon — ​belongs ‌to ​the ​Slavic tradition, ‌where ​it ‌is ​catalogued under ‌the ​domain ​"Three-Headed ​Dragon". ​The name ​means ‌"Mountain ​dragon".

‌**Zmey Gorynych** ​is ‌three-headed ​dragon. ‌The ​name means ‌"Mountain ​dragon" ​and ‌belongs to ‌the ‌slavic ​tradition.

​PuniCodex restores ‌the ​name ​as ‌**Zmey ​Gorynych** and ​serves ‌its ​temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/zmeygorynych/). ​The ​restoration ​needs ‌no distinctive ‌letters ​or ‌diacritics ​its ASCII ​form ‌would ‌lose, ‌which places ‌the ​name ‌in ​Tier ​2. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form ​*zmeygorynych* survives ​as ‌a ​modern ​convenience ​imposed by ‌the ​early ‌domain-name ​system; the ‌restoration, ​not ‌the ‌fallback, is ​the ​form ​the ​project ‌defends as ‌philologically ​complete.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation survives ‌for this ​name; **Zmey ​Gorynych** is ​a scholarly ​transliteration of ​the ‌reconstructed spoken ​form. Etymologically ​the name ‌means "Mountain ​dragon".

The ‌ASCII form ​*zmeygorynych* survives ‌only ​because the ​early domain-name ​system could ​not carry ​diacritics; it ‌is a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Zmey Gorynych** ​recovers the ‌full diacritic ​detail of ​the ‌scholarly transliteration ‌directly in ‌the address ​bar. The ​restoration needs ‌no distinctive ​letters or ​diacritics ‌its ASCII ​form would ​lose, which ‌places the ​name in ‌Tier 2.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**z** → ‌**Z** — ‌Same, capitalized
​- **m** ‌→ **m** ​— Same
​- ‌**e** → ‌**e** — ‌Same
- ‌**y** → ​**y** — ‌Same
- ​**g** → ​**G** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**o** → ​**o** — ​Same
- ‌**r** → ​**r** — ​Same
​- **y** ‌→ **y** ​— Same
‌- **n** ​→ **n** ‌— Same
​- **y** ‌→ ‌**y** — ​Same
- ​**c** → ​**c** — ​Same
- ‌**h** → ‌**h** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/zmeygorynych/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly form.

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

‌- **zmeygorynych** ​— ‌The ​canonical restored ‌form ​Zmey ​Gorynych.

​For the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation ‌is: ​Say "zmeygorynych" ‌with ​the ‌stress ​and length ‌implied ​by ​the scholarly ‌restoration ‌"Zmey ‌Gorynych".

​The ASCII ​form ‌"zmeygorynych" ​is a ​DNS ‌compromise; ​the restoration ​"Zmey ‌Gorynych" ​preserves ‌the name's ​scholarly ​dignity.

​The pronunciation ​given ‌above ‌reconstructs the ​sound ‌world ​in ​which Zmey ‌Gorynych ‌was ‌invoked. Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not ​expect exact ​identity ​with ‌ancient phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not ​a performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌restoration Zmey ​Gorynych ‌keeps ​the ‌prosodic information ‌visible ​even ​when the ​name ​is ‌typed in ‌plain ​ASCII.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Zmey ‌Gorynych ​place three-headed ​dragon ​at the ​center ​of a ‌living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

Zmey ‌Gorynych ​appears in ‌slavic ​tradition ​as three-headed ​dragon. ​The name's ​meaning, ‌"Mountain ​dragon", shapes ‌the ​narratives told ‌about ​this figure.

‌### ​Worship ‌and Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Zmey ​Gorynych ​in ritual, ‌text, ​and iconography, ​ensuring ‌the ​name survived ​into ‌the modern ​scholarly ‌record.

The ​myths ​of ​Zmey Gorynych ​survive ‌in fragments, ‌summaries, ​and ‌later retellings. ​Each ​version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ​— poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does ​not privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare them. ‌The ​restoration ‌Zmey Gorynych ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is yet ​assigned ​to ‌Zmey ​Gorynych ‌with ​certainty. That ‌absence ​should ​be ​read ​honestly: ​for a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it would ‌take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory inscriptions ‌naming ‌Zmey ‌Gorynych, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​three-headed ‌dragon ​and iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes ​(name ​and domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To ​contemplate ‌Zmey Gorynych ‌is ​to ​hold ​the ​idea of ​three-Headed ‌Dragon ​in ​the ‌mind and ​to ‌ask ​what ‌of it ​endures. ​The ​name ​means ​"Mountain dragon" ‌— ​and ‌a ​name that ‌carries ​its ‌meaning ​so ‌openly invites ​meditation ​rather ‌than ‌mere ‌recollection. The ​tradition ​remembers ‌the ​name as ​three-Headed ‌Dragon ​· ​Mountain ‌dragon.

Sit ​with ‌the ​restored ​form ​— Zmey ​Gorynych ‌— ‌and ​the diacritics ‌themselves ​become ​the ‌practice: ‌each mark ‌is ‌a ​small ‌act ​of attention, ​a ​refusal ‌to ​let the ​plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*zmeygorynych* ​stand in ​for ‌the ​whole. ‌What the ​tradition ‌preserved ​in ‌this ‌name, the ​restoration ​asks ​the ​reader ‌to preserve ‌in ​turn.
